tldr: We introduce the Riemannian MeanFlow Policy (RMFP), which eliminates the need for multi-step numerical integration in diffusion and flow-based policies while preserving geometric constraints (manifolds) such as robot end-effector poses. Through teacher-free, single-stage training, it generates action trajectories with just a single network function evaluation (1-NFE) that rival existing multi-step approaches.
hero_caption: 1-NFE trajectory generation results for the LASA letter "W" on the sphere $\mathcal{S}^2$. Black lines denote demonstrations, and colored lines show generated trajectories. Compared to conventional RFMP (left), the proposed RMFP (right) generates smooth trajectories faithful to the demonstrations with a single function evaluation.
overview:
In visuomotor policies where robots directly output action sequences from sensory observations like images, diffusion models and flow matching are widely used to capture multimodal action distributions. However, they suffer from a serious limitation: generating an action requires numerically integrating the learned vector field (solving an ODE), which drives up the number of network function evaluations (NFE) and slows down control rates. Furthermore, robot end-effector poses (position, orientation quaternion, and gripper state) live on Riemannian manifolds rather than Euclidean space, requiring action generation that respects these geometric constraints.

To solve this, the authors propose the Riemannian MeanFlow Policy (RMFP), which directly learns the conditioned flow map (average velocity) representing finite-time transport on the manifold rather than an instantaneous velocity field. By combining a flow map consistency loss grounded in an algebraic semigroup property with a Riemannian conditional flow matching anchor tied to demonstration data, this framework enables stable, single-stage training without teacher distillation or higher-order derivative terms.

Evaluations span spherical letter trajectories (LASA), Push-T, Robomimic in Euclidean space, Franka Kitchen with an end-effector pose manifold ($\mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathcal{S}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^2$), and real-world experiments on a 6-DoF manipulator. Across all setups, RMFP achieves high task success rates matching or exceeding prior multi-step methods requiring 10+ NFE, all at a minimal compute cost of just 1 to 2 NFE.
contributions: Formulating RMFP, a teacher-free, single-stage framework that directly learns flow maps on product action manifolds by combining algebraic semigroup consistency with Riemannian conditional flow matching

Designing two network output parameterizations—velocity-predictive and endpoint-predictive—which enforce manifold constraints at different points, and theoretically and empirically characterizing their behavior across dimensions and tasks

Demonstrating performance competitive with SOTA multi-step generative methods at very low compute budgets (1–2 NFE) across spherical, product manifold, and Euclidean simulation benchmarks, as well as on a real-world robot

sections.heading: Why is fast 1-step generation on manifolds necessary?
sections.summary: Robot action spaces are geometric manifolds containing rotations and other constraints, yet conventional diffusion and flow-based policies require multi-step numerical integration, impeding high-frequency control. This paper extends the concept of MeanFlow—enabling finite-time jumps—to manifolds, proposing RMFP for teacher-free, single-stage training.
sections.details:
In robot visuomotor policy learning, multiple valid solutions often exist for the same observation, making diffusion models and flow matching standard backbones for modeling multimodal distributions. However, the action space composed of robot end-effector positions, quaternion orientations, and gripper states is not a simple vector space, but a product manifold such as $\mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathcal{S}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^2$. Forcing this into a flat 9-dimensional Euclidean space places probability mass on physically meaningless off-manifold regions.

The previous Riemannian Flow Matching Policy (RFMP) learns velocity fields along geodesics on the manifold as conditional paths. Yet inference requires solving numerical integrations (such as Euler steps) repeatedly, scaling inference latency with the number of network function evaluations (NFE). Coarsening integration steps readily causes mode collapse on manifolds, demanding per-task step tuning.

To tackle this bottleneck, learning flow maps that directly jump across finite time intervals in very few steps has gained traction. However, existing consistency models require distillation from pre-trained teachers, and prior MeanFlow approaches were restricted to Euclidean spaces or biomolecular data. RMFP directly learns the flow map (interval average velocity) on the robot's action manifold, enabling highly accurate action generation with as few as 1 NFE in a single, teacher-free training stage.

Black lines show demonstration trajectories, and colored lines show generated ones. While RFMP (left) becomes jagged and incurs large errors due to coarse integration, RMFP (right) reproduces the demonstrations smoothly in a single step.

sections.heading: The evolution of generative models on manifolds and robot action learning
sections.summary: We review the progress of generative models on Riemannian manifolds (normalizing flows, diffusion models, flow matching) and efforts to reduce NFE in robot manipulation. This work marks the first application of flow map learning to product action manifolds in robotics.
sections.details:
### II-A Generative Models on Riemannian Manifolds
Efforts to build generative models on manifolds have included continuous normalizing flows based on manifold-constrained ODEs and diffusion models based on heat kernels. Riemannian Flow Matching (RFM) then emerged, regressing velocity fields along geodesic paths without requiring divergence estimation or complex simulations. However, all these approaches rely on vector field integration, resulting in slow sampling. Recent concurrent work has explored learning flow maps directly, but these target geographic data or protein structures and have not been applied to observation-conditioned action sequence generation in robotics.

### II-B Generative Policy Learning for Robot Manipulation
In robot manipulation, Diffusion Policy has shown strong performance by generating action chunks (sequences of actions over time) all at once. To accelerate sampling, step-adaptive solvers, distillation techniques like Consistency Policy, and Euclidean flow map learning have been studied. However, no prior approach enabled teacher-free, derivative-free, 1-step generation while explicitly respecting manifold constraints like rotations.

sections.heading: Capturing average velocity on manifolds via semigroup consistency and anchors
sections.summary: RMFP learns the average velocity representing transport along probability paths. It trains in a single stage with first-order gradients only, using no teacher model by combining an algebraic semigroup consistency loss (stating that composing two intermediate moves equals the overall transport) with a flow matching anchor tied to data.
sections.details:
### III-A Geometric Background and RFMP
Representing robot end-effector actions $\mathcal{A} = \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathcal{S}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^2$ over a horizon $T_p$ yields the product manifold $\mathcal{M} = \mathcal{A}^{T_p}$. Geodesics are defined via the exponential map $\mathrm{Exp}$ and logarithmic map $\mathrm{Log}$. Conventional RFMP learns the instantaneous velocity $v(a, s)$ along geodesics from a prior distribution to demonstration actions, requiring $T$ exponential Euler updates ($T$ NFE) during sampling.

### III-B Riemannian MeanFlow Policy (RMFP) Formulation
To predict movement over a finite interval $[s, t]$ in a single step, RMFP considers the average velocity $u(a, s, t) = \frac{\mathrm{Log}_a(\Phi_{s,t}(a))}{t-s}$, which scales the geodesic chord by the time interval. For any intermediate time $s \le r \le t$, the flow map satisfies the composition rule $\Phi_{r,t} \circ \Phi_{s,r} = \Phi_{s,t}$. Using this algebraic semigroup identity as a target, we define the consistency loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{semi}}$ with a stop-gradient ($\mathrm{sg}$).

Because the semigroup property can be trivially satisfied by $u \equiv 0$, we couple it with a Riemannian conditional flow matching anchor loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{anchor}}$ at the limit $t=s$ to anchor the boundary to the demonstration data. This allows stable training using only first-order gradients, without any higher-order derivative terms like Jacobian-vector products.

### Output Parameterizations (Velocity vs. Endpoint Prediction)
Two architectures enforce manifold constraints on the network output $h_\theta$:
- **Velocity Prediction (RMF-$v$)**: Projects the network output orthogonally onto the tangent space $T_a\mathcal{M}$ to produce $u_\theta$.
- **Endpoint Prediction (RMF-$x_1$)**: Projects the output directly onto the manifold $\mathcal{M}$, then back-calculates the average velocity along the geodesic. A weighting function handles the singularity caused by the $1-s$ term in the denominator.

### Implementation Details
The backbone uses a 1D-UNet standard in Diffusion Policy, with observations conditioned via FiLM. The time input is expanded to receive two timesteps, $(s, t)$.

sections.heading: How close can 1-step generation get to multi-step methods?
sections.summary: Experiments were conducted on spherical LASA, spherical Push-T, Franka Kitchen, Robomimic, and a real robot. At ultra-low compute budgets of 1 to 2 NFE, RMFP significantly outperforms conventional RFMP and diffusion models, achieving performance on par with 10-NFE baselines.
sections.details:
### IV-A & B Benchmark Results
- **Spherical LASA (Letter Trajectory Generation)**: At $\mathrm{NFE}=1$, the median DTW error was $0.022$ for RMF-$x_1$ and $0.033$ for RMF-$v$, vastly outperforming RFMP ($0.090$) with smooth and highly accurate trajectories.
- **Spherical Push-T**: At $\mathrm{NFE}=1$, RMF-$v$ attained a coverage score of $78.5$, substantially ahead of RFMP ($67.9$) and the diffusion baseline RDP-$x$ ($73.1$). At $\mathrm{NFE}=10$, it reached $85.0$.
- **Franka Kitchen ($\mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathcal{S}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^2$)**: Evaluated on achieving 4 or more subtasks. At $\mathrm{NFE}=1$, RMF-$x_1$-hemi (hemisphere prior) achieved $41.7$, outpacing RFMP-hemi ($20.6$) by a margin of $21.1$ points. Endpoint prediction (RMF-$x_1$) proved especially robust on high-dimensional product manifolds.
- **Robomimic (Euclidean Space)**: On Tool Hang (7-DoF), RMF-$v$ achieved a $64.0$ success rate at $\mathrm{NFE}=1$ (standard Diffusion Policy collapsed at $0.0$). On Transport (14-DoF bimanual), it maintained over $90.0$ success with just 1 NFE.

Overall, increasing NFE from 1 to 10 led to performance variations of at most $10.2$ points across settings, showing an extremely flat, robust profile unaffected by low computational budgets.

### IV-C Real-World Robot Verification
Using a physical 6-DoF I2RT YAM arm powered by an NVIDIA Jetson Thor, a pick-and-place manipulation task was evaluated under multimodal sensing from external and wrist cameras. Trained on 60 demonstrations, RMFP generated smooth, real-time, non-divergent actions even under real-world sensor noise.

captions.F4: Execution phases of real-world manipulation with the 6-DoF robot arm (YAM). Approaching a block on the table, grasping it, transporting it to the goal location, and placing it accurately into the box are executed smoothly and at high speed using the learned RMFP.

sections.heading: A new standard for fast policies with geometric constraints
sections.summary: By integrating algebraic semigroup consistency with flow matching anchors, RMFP dramatically lowers the inference cost of action generation on manifolds. With teacher-free, single-stage training using only first-order gradients, it delivers 1-NFE action generation—an ideal trait for robotic control.
sections.details: This work overcomes the multi-step integration bottleneck in geometrically constrained visuomotor policies by learning finite-time average velocities (flow maps) instead of traditional instantaneous velocity fields. The algebraic consistency loss eliminates derivative calculations and circumvents teacher distillation, keeping implementation and training overhead low. Generating manifold-constrained action sequences in a single forward pass provides a highly practical foundation for real-world robotics where high-rate control loops are essential.

takeaways: Even on manifold spaces like robot end-effector poses, solving flow map consistency (semigroup property) makes 1-step action generation viable for practical use.
Without distilling from a teacher model, combining a data-boundary anchor loss with the semigroup loss enables stable single-stage training using only first-order gradients.

Network output parameterization matters: velocity prediction (RMF-v) tends to excel in lower dimensions, while endpoint prediction (RMF-x1) is advantageous on high-dimensional product manifolds containing orientations.
limitations: Evaluating the semigroup property requires four network evaluations per gradient step during training, making the training compute heavier than standard RFMP (which uses one evaluation).
Scaling to 5–10 NFE does not significantly exceed the performance ceiling of conventional multi-step flow matching (RFMP); its primary strength lies in preserving performance in the low-NFE regime.
The formulation is restricted to spaces where logarithmic and exponential maps can be computed in closed (analytic) form, such as spheres and products of Euclidean spaces.
